catalog_quote: 16. The place of the primary accent, which in Classic Latin was determined by quantity, remained unchanged in Vulgar Latin even after quantitative distinctions were lost. A short vowel before a mute followed by a liquid may, in Classic Latin, be stressed or unstressed; in Vulgar Latin it is usually stressed: cathédra, tenébræ. ... 17. In Provençal the primary accent falls on the same syllable as in Vulgar Latin: bonitātem > V. L. bonitáte > Pr. bontát, compŭtum > V. L. cómputu > Pr. cónte; cathĕdra > V. audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim on the held page image (p. 12, sec. 17) and in the held scanned text (secs. 16-19, pp. 11-13). (2) Deciding source is a 1905 historical grammar; for an extinct medieval language that is the appropriate genre, and three independent historical grammars fetched sources now (Schultz-Gora 1906 sec. 15, Appel 1918 sec. 21 p. 25, Anglade 1921 pp. 42-43, the last being Glottolog's listed grammar) state the identical rule: Old Provençal stress sits on the syllable that bore the Latin accent, with listed lexical exceptions (learned words, foreign names oxytone, analogical verb shifts, rhyme licences). That supports the LEXICAL coding (position etymologically given; both oxytones and paroxytones occur with the same final shapes, e.g. sénher vs molhér). (3) Only real gap is Paden 1998, the modern 610-pp reference, not open; unlikely to overturn the coding. (4) Status adequate; action

sources.citation: Anglade, Joseph. 1921. Grammaire de l'ancien provençal ou ancienne langue d'oc: phonétique et morphologie. Paris: Klincksieck. (archive.org grammairedelanci00angl)
sources.quote: 'Sauf ces dérogations à la règle générale, qui s'expliquent d'ailleurs par la phonétique, la syllabe qui porte l'accent en latin la conserve en provençal comme dans les autres langues romanes.' Preceding pages list the Vulgar Latin shifts (pariétem, muliérem, filiólum, cathédram, recomposition renégat), Old Prov. shifts in -ánum place names, learned words stressed on the final per the Leys d'Amors (gramatíca, Semiramís), and troubadour rhyme-driven shifts.

sources.citation: Appel, Carl. 1918. Provenzalische Lautlehre. Leipzig: Reisland. (archive.org provenzalischela00appe)
sources.quote: 'Der Ton liegt im Provenzalischen auf der Silbe, welche der lateinischen betonten entspricht.' Adds VL intégrum/tenébrae/filiólum shifts, clitic destressing (ama'l filh), and that consonant-final learned words/foreign names were pronounced oxytone (París, Cesár, esperít) with vacillation for vowel-final ones, citing Leys d'Amors I 90.

sources.citation: Schultz-Gora, Oskar. 1906. Altprovenzalisches Elementarbuch. Heidelberg: Winter. (archive.org altprovenzalisch00schuuoft)
sources.quote: 'In volkstümlichen Wörtern ... bleibt der Platz des lateinischen Akzentes fast ausnahmslos bewahrt'; secs. 16-18 list analogical shifts in verb forms, Latin word-forms and foreign names stressed on the last syllable (Dominí, Biblís), and rhyme-driven shifts by troubadours.
